result:
The proposed answer of 8 is not justified, so I reject it.

**The square-antiprism argument is unsupported.** The solution never constructs the conflict graph or checks its cuts. It says it "can be proven" that some perfect matching hits every edge cut, but gives no matching and no proof. It also claims the square antiprism is "widely known in graph theory literature" as the unique exception, which I cannot verify and which the solution does not cite.

**The octahedron analysis is also flawed.** It shows that one particular family of matchings (stars at vertices) fails to hit a triangle cut. It then concludes that the octahedron is not exceptional because "for any 1-regular conflict graph, one can always find a conflict-free cut." Failure of one matching does not establish that every matching fails. Its own reasoning shows that hitting all six vertex-star cuts forces a specific structure: each vertex's matched pair is two of its incident edges, with each edge in exactly one pair. That amounts to an orientation of the octahedron in which every vertex has out-degree 2. The solution never tests whether any such orientation also hits all the other bonds.

I checked part of this by hand. I found one orientation that hits all six star cuts and one of the four opposite-face-pair cuts, but it misses the others. That does not settle the question, since I did not check every orientation or every bond. It does suggest the octahedron is a serious candidate for the exception, which would make the answer 6 rather than 8. I have not verified that conclusion, and I am not certain of it.

The final answer of 8 rests on an unproven assertion, so it cannot be accepted.

VERDICT: REJECT
